newsitem.title: DENMARK: Baltic sea states, U.S. discuss regional defence.
newsitem.headline: Baltic sea states, U.S. discuss regional defence.

text.p: Defence ministers, officials and academics gather on Monday for Baltic Sea security talks expected to focus on bringing three Baltic republics closer to NATO during what may be long waiting period for membership.
The Copenhagen seminar brings together NATO, non-aligned and former Warsaw Pact states to discuss a delicate issue in relations between Russia and the West.

Russia is nervous of NATO enlargement on its borders, while it is precisely the former Soviet republics and satellites who feel most in need of security guarantees, given their huge and volatile neighbour.

Scheduled speakers include U.S. Defence Secretary William Perry, British Defence Minister Michael Portillo, his German counterpart, Volker Ruehe and Russian Baltic Fleet Commander Admiral W.G.Yegorov.
The two-day seminar is a closed-door affair on which the Danish hosts are maintaining an uncharacteristic news blackout.
"The parties decided to exclude the press so that officials and academics could have a free exchange of views," a defence ministry official said.
Also attending are defence Ministers from the Baltic republics, Denmark, Finland, Sweden and the Netherlands and senior officials from Poland and Norway.

Denmark, a founder member of NATO and home to its Baltic regional headquarters (BALTAP) is an impassioned advocate of expanding the alliance, as Defence Minister Hans Haekkerup made clear in a June address to a NATO workshop in Warsaw.

"Denmark had the benefits of the security guarantee as a member of NATO when it was a frontline state. If I were to deny new, stable democracies in central and eastern Europe the same security guarantees I would have a moral problem," he said.
The three Baltic states, which have geographical proximity and cultural links with the Nordic countries, are unlikely to be among the first eastern countries to join NATO.
The first wave is expected to consist of the Czech Republic, Hungary, Poland and Slovakia.

NATO is seen as unwilling to provoke Russia, whose worries about eastward NATO expansion are exacerbated in the case of the Baltic states by Moscow's proprietorial attitude toward large Russian minorities there, particularly Estonia and Latvia.

A defence analyst, who asked not to be identified, said that a Danish proposal to help gently integrate the three republics, which seceded from the Soviet Union in 1991, was that through NATO's Partnership for Peace they should be tied into BALTAP.

"They would simply be there and participate in everything. This is as close as you can get to membership," he said. "Denmark has virtually been running this show since the beginning so these countries have some confidence in Denmark."
"That initiative has a lot of American backing and I see the seminar as a way of promoting these ideas," he added.

Dr. Pertti Jonnieni of Copenhagen's Centre for Peace and Conflict Research, a government-aided think-tank, said another key aim was to build on projects such as Russian, Baltic, Nordic and NATO cooperation in Bosnian peacekeeping.

"The purpose is to create frameworks where the Russians and the Balts more and more encounter each other and learn to deal and cope with each other...so that instead of increasing the distance between the Russians and the Balts the measures are aiming at decreasing the distance," he said.
Officials say that the seminar is meant as an exchange of views and no agreements are expected. Russia has sent a relatively low-level delegation.
The NATO ministers continue on Tuesday to Norway where they will meet for two days and be joined by Russian defence Minister Igor Rodinov.
